newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco stocks tumble on litigation woes.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco stocks tumble on litigation woes.

text.p: Tobacco stocks were down sharply at midday Thursday amid fears that Mississippi Gov. Kirk Fordice's legal challenge to a landmark tobacco lawsuit brought by his state's attorney general is headed for defeat.

The skid also came amid news that Liggett Group Inc, a unit of Brook Group Ltd, was preparing to expand its negotiated settlement of tobacco liability suits to dozens of other states that have sued the industry since Liggett first struck its settlement almost a year ago.

On the New York Stock Exchange, shares of Philip Morris Cos Inc were down five points at 131-1/4. RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp was off 1-3/8 at 34-3/4, and Loews Corp traded at 107-1/8, down 3-1/4. Other stocks were also lower.

Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore told Reuters Thursday that he had no indication that a ruling on his suit would come from the Mississippi Supreme Court today, but said court rulings are released on Thursdays at 1430 EST.1930 GMT.
Moore's suit seeks compensation for state Medicaid funds spent treating poor people for smoking-related illnesses.
Fordice, a Republican, sued to block Moore's suit, alleging that Moore, a Democrat, did not have the authority to bring the litigation.

Analysts also pointed to other factors that could have weighed on tobacco shares, including today's ex-dividend date for Philip Morris and a general day of red ink for consumer stocks overall. But analysts cited the Mississippi rumors as a likely cause.
Smith Barney analyst Martin Feldman said that even if the governor's challenge is blocked, "it does not comment on the industry's defenses."
"I would not expect Philip Morris to fall more than five dollars" in share price, Feldman said.

Paine Webber's Emanuel Goldman said the threat that Liggett will release industry documents that imply a higher degree of industry culpability in personal injuries was toothless, because the documents "are nothing."
"Even with those documents, you have to prove fraud at the highest level (of a tobacco company), and that's the hard part here," Goldman said.
